source.title_on_document: CreAItive Collaboration? Users' Misjudgment of AI-Creativity Affects Their Collaborative Performance

supplement.where: The paper refers to 'Supplementary Materials' (pp. 5, 6, 7, 10) and gives no URL or file name.
supplement.holds: Interface screenshots and descriptions, the informed consent form, all questionnaires, the detailed AUT scoring description, detailed descriptive statistics of the sample with the bias analyses, and two exemplary human-AI interactions (pp. 5-7, 10). For the AUT outcomes, the main text prints standard deviations only for immediate post-test fluency and for the top-quartile comparisons (pp. 8-9). Whether the supplement contains coder identities, coding reliability, or standard deviations and test statistics for the remaining AUT outcomes is not stated; the supplement was not available for inspection.

paper_design_summary: Dyads were randomly assigned on arrival to ChatGPT-4 access or no AI during three four-minute Alternate Uses Test (AUT) items; the experiment analyzed 104 second-semester Computer Science students in 52 dyads, with 26 dyads per arm (pp. 5-6, Sections 4.2-4.3). The authors scored fluency, flexibility, originality, and elaboration in the main test, an unaided immediate dyad post-test, and an individual online unaided retention post-test three weeks later (pp. 6-7). The paper also summarizes a separately published pre-study comparing 10 AI chatbots with 20 human dyads (p. 4, Section 4.1).

arms.name: Experimental AI group
arms.description: Dyads did the three main-test AUT items (fork, flower pot, suitcase; four minutes each) with off-the-shelf ChatGPT-4 in a chat window of the task interface. Copy-paste from the chat into the answer box was disabled. ChatGPT-4 was removed for the immediate and retention post-tests.

arms.name: Control non-AI group
arms.description: Dyads did the same three main-test AUT items in the same interface without AI, then the same unaided post-tests.

participants.exclusions: The analyzed valid sample was 52 dyads (104 participants), 26 dyads (52 participants) per condition (p. 6, Section 4.3). Only native or advanced German-speaking dyads entered the final sample (p. 5, Section 4.2.1); the numbers tested, randomized, and excluded are not stated. Retention attrition is not reported: Figure 1 shows 52 vs 52 individuals, while Figure 12 labels the retention means as 26 vs 26 dyads (pp. 5, 10).
participants.who: Second-semester Computer Science students from an introductory lecture on data science and AI, aged 18 to 35 (mean 21.55), 77.88 percent male. 99.04 percent had used generative AI before. Participants earned a 5 percent course-grade bonus. Dyads formed themselves by booking a shared slot.
participants.quote: The valid sample consisted of 52 dyads/104 participants, with 26 dyads/52 participants per experimental condition.
participants.locator: p. 6, Section 4.3 (Sample); recruitment p. 5, Section 4.2.1; Figure 1, p. 5

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT-4, off the shelf, used as is without prompt engineering by the research team. The Methods give no model version. Reference [80], cited for ChatGPT in general on p. 1, reads 'Model: gpt-4, version: March 2024'.
ai_tool.how_used: A chat window inside the AUT interface. Dyads prompted ChatGPT-4 freely while working together on a shared display. Copy-paste from the chat into the answer box was blocked, so dyads typed any AI answer they kept (pp. 5-6, Sections 4.2.2 and 4.4.1). AI was available only during the three main-test items and was removed for both post-tests (pp. 5-6, Sections 4.2-4.2.4). Dyads accepted 32.91 percent of AI-generated uses, and entered answers were 49.96 percent AI-generated (p. 12, Table 5). The text reports 40.90 percent accepted after excluding already-written and no-time answers (p. 11, Section 5.3); that figure is not printed in Table 5.

task.description: Alternate Uses Test done collaboratively by dyads on a shared display. Main test: fork, flower pot, suitcase (AI group with ChatGPT-4). Unaided immediate post-test: glass bottle (dyads, no AI). Unaided retention post-test three weeks later: key, brick, gymnastics ball (individuals, online, no AI).
task.duration: Four minutes per AUT item. The on-campus session (main test plus immediate post-test) lasted about one hour. Retention post-test three weeks later.

outcomes.name: AUT flexibility, main test (with AI)

outcomes.measure_detail: Number of different categories among a dyad's alternate uses, 1 point per category (scoring after Alhashim et al. 2020, done by the authors), dyad mean index over the three main-test items. Top-quartile means are also reported. The main text does not identify individual coders or report coding reliability. It refers only a detailed description of AUT scoring to the Supplementary Materials; their coverage of coder identity and reliability is unknown (p. 7, Section 4.5.1).

S2 summarizes the pre-study published separately as Bangerl, Stefan, and Pammer-Schindler (2024), 'Explorations in human vs. Generative AI creative performances: A study on human-AI creative potential', CHI TREW 2024 workshop paper (reference [7]).

company_involvement.description: No AI-company involvement stated, and ChatGPT-4 was used off the shelf. Three authors (Bangerl, Disch, Pammer-Schindler) list Know Center Research GmbH, a research center in Graz, beside Graz University of Technology. eligibility.reason: S1 meets all three criteria: dyads were randomly assigned on arrival to ChatGPT-4 access or no AI on the AUT (p. 5, Section 4.2.2); 104 people in 52 dyads were analyzed, with 52 people/26 dyads per arm (p. 6, Section 4.3); and the submitted AUT answers were scored for fluency, flexibility, originality, and elaboration (p. 7, Section 4.5.1). The unknown pre-exclusion randomized count, uncertain statistical units, missing precision, coder details, and retention reporting do not remove those main-test facts. S2 is separately published AI-versus-human context without random assignment of human AI assistance; unresolved S2 counts and population details do not determine core eligibility.

one_line_finding: The paper reports no significant main-test differences in AUT fluency (14.6 vs 12.7), originality (3.7 vs 3.7), or flexibility (10.0 vs 9.4), but lower AI-group elaboration immediately (2.1 vs 3.8; U = 924.0, p = 0.005) and after AI removal (2.8 vs 4.7; U = 970.0, p = 0.012), with no significant retention difference three weeks later (1.9 vs 2.2), although the elaboration tests have unresolved analysis units (pp. 8-10, Sections 5.1.1-5.1.3 and Figures 4, 8, 12).
open_questions: S1 statistical units: elaboration U = 924.0 in the main test and U = 970.0 in the immediate post-test exceed the mathematical maximum 26 x 26 = 676 for the stated dyad counts (pp. 8-9, Sections 5.1.1-5.1.2). Figure 14 labels the correlation as 26 AI dyads, but the printed rho_s = 0.424, p = 0.002 does not match the usual two-sided approximation with that count (p. 11, Section 5.3 and Figure 14). Duplicated participant rows are a possible explanation, not a documented fact; another analysis unit, test convention, or reporting error is also possible. The authors or analysis files are needed to establish the units and obtain valid dyad-level precision. This affects statistical extraction, not the three eligibility criteria.

S1 retention sample and analysis unit: Figure 1 shows 52 vs 52 individuals, while Figure 12 labels the means as 26 vs 26 dyads; no retention attrition count is reported (pp. 5, 9-10, Figure 1, Section 5.1.3, Figure 12). Authors or analysis records must confirm how many people were analyzed and whether individual scores or dyad averages entered the analysis. This does not change eligibility established by the main test.

S1 randomized and excluded counts: the numbers randomized before the German-language inclusion rule and excluded afterward are not stated; the analyzed valid sample is 52 dyads/104 people (pp. 5-6, Sections 4.2.1-4.3). Authors must supply the participant flow. Random assignment and the analyzed count above 50 are already confirmed, so these missing counts do not change eligibility.

S1 missing dispersion and test statistics: most AUT outcomes have only figure means and statements about significance; standard deviations are printed only for immediate post-test fluency and the top-quartile comparisons (pp. 8-10). Inspect the supplement for additional statistics; its statistical coverage is not stated, and author-provided analysis results may still be needed. The preregistration is not evidence of observed standard deviations. Missing precision does not affect eligibility.

S1 coder identities and reliability: the main text describes scoring and coding but does not identify individual coders or report reliability (p. 7, Sections 4.5.1-4.5.2). Inspect the detailed scoring description in the supplement; the paper does not say whether it resolves these details. Output scoring itself is confirmed, so eligibility is unaffected.

S1 unaided retention compliance: the online individual test is described as without ChatGPT-4, but how AI use during the test was prevented or checked is unstated; the interim AI-use questionnaire results are not reported (pp. 5-6, Sections 4.2 and 4.2.4). Authors must clarify compliance checks and the questionnaire results. This affects the retention after_ai interpretation, not main-test eligibility.

S2 direct people count and population: c032 reports 20 dyads and defines a dyad as two humans (p. 4, Sections 3 and 4.1), but gives no separate people count or demographic description. The checker reports 40 students, mostly psychology students at an Austrian university, from reference [7]. The cited PDF and an OpenAlex fallback both failed because network sockets were denied, and no local primary copy was found. Obtain the original pre-study from its authors before adding those details. S2 is AI-versus-human context and does not determine core eligibility.

S2 observation unit and n_units: c032 reports 10 chatbots and 20 human dyads but does not explicitly identify the observations entering its pre-study U tests (p. 4, Section 4.1). The proposed 30 producer scores and the prior team-only coding are not independently confirmed. The original pre-study or author-provided analysis details must establish the test units. Core eligibility rests on S1 and is unaffected.
notes: The preregistered hypotheses H1-H3 concern flexibility and originality only (p. 4; preregistration also discussed in Section 6.4, pp. 13-14), so those outcomes are marked preregistered_primary and fluency and elaboration secondary. The control group was significantly older (U = 1038.5, p = 0.038), and the AI group reported more frequent private AI use (U = 1631.0, p = 0.040); the authors report no confounding effects in correlation and moderation checks (p. 6, Section 4.3). Process results: dyads accepted 32.91 percent of AI-generated uses, and entered answers were 49.96 percent AI-generated (p. 12, Table 5). The 40.90 percent acceptance figure excluding already-written and no-time answers is printed in the text (p. 11, Section 5.3), not Table 5. The acceptance-rate correlation with main-test fluency is reported as rho_s = 0.424, p = 0.002 (p. 11, Section 5.3); Figure 14 labels it as 26 dyads, but the p-value does not match the usual two-sided approximation at that count. This is an audit inconsistency, not proof that scores were duplicated; the correlation and elaboration tests must not be treated as confirmed dyad-level inference without analysis details. Prompt-specificity results (Tables 3-4) and perception-of-AI questionnaire results (Section 5.2, Figure 13) are process or self-report measures and are not coded as outcomes. Originality is scored by rarity within the cohort, a property of each output, so it is coded novelty and the paper has no across_people outcome. The authors do not compare retention scores with earlier phases because the retention test was individual (p. 7). Sections 4.5.1 and 4.5.2 print the same text twice (p. 7). The inner title of Figure 11 reads 'Main Test: Elaboration Distribution' while its caption says immediate post-test (p. 10). S1 is the original randomized experiment; S2 summarizes an AI-versus-human comparison with no assignment of human AI assistance and retains design_class ai_vs_human. The reconciliation object is preserved as historical provenance. Its claims that coder identities/reliability are deferred to the supplement, that S2 has a confirmed team-level test unit, and that its 20 dyads fill people-count fields are superseded by the final resolutions. The full markdown and the PDF passages and figures supporting recorded results were checked. No supplement or original pre-study PDF was available; no external demographic or sample-size claims were adopted without primary-source verification.

differences.resolved: team: one score per producer, 20 dyads against 10 chatbots. The paper does not name the unit, but the printed statistics fit only that comparison. U can be at most 10 x 20 = 200, and U = 147.0 and U = 25.0 give p of about 0.04 and 0.001 under the normal approximation, as printed. A test over single uses would have many more units, and these U values would then give far smaller p-values.

Retained rho_s = 0.424 and p = 0.002 exactly as printed and the figure's 26-dyad label. open_items.item: S1 elaboration-test and Figure 14 correlation units need author clarification and dyad-level analysis results; the concern affects precision, not random assignment, analyzed people, or output scoring.
S1 retention count, attrition, and individual-versus-dyad analysis need confirmation; main-test eligibility is already established.
S1 numbers randomized and excluded under the language rule need participant-flow records; 104 analyzed people and stated random assignment already meet criteria 1 and 2.
S1 missing AUT standard deviations and test statistics require inspection of the supplement; its coverage is unknown, and authors may still be needed. This affects effect extraction only.
S1 coder identities and reliability require inspection of the supplement scoring description; its coverage is unknown. The paper already confirms output scoring.
S1 retention AI-use prevention/checks and interim AI-use questionnaire results require author clarification; this affects the after_ai interpretation, not main-test eligibility.
S2 direct people count, population, and country require the original pre-study from its authors; only 20 dyads are directly reported in c032. S2 does not determine core eligibility.
S2 observation unit and proposed 30 producer-score observations require the original pre-study or author-provided analysis details; the c032 summary does not settle them.
